ALG-H4-11.new_tell: Mild, not disqualifying. Two things. (1) Every option is a multiple of 6 and two of the three distractors are one arithmetic step from the stem's own numbers (48 = 60 - 12, 30 = 60/2); the key is not, so a student running 'the answer is the option you cannot build in one move from the given numbers' narrows to {42, 54} for free. (2) In a 'greatest possible value' question the smallest option (30) is the psychologically cheapest to drop, and it is also the degenerate equal-split case, so the effective field is closer to three options than four. Neither identifies the key without algebra.
ALG-H4-11.note: Repair holds on the point it was made for: the feasible set is genuinely bounded above. Because the comparison is 'at least' (3s >= L + 12, closed), the supremum L = 42 is ATTAINED at s = 18, so 'greatest possible value' is well posed. A strict 'more than' here would have left no greatest value at all - that is the failure mode this now avoids, and it is worth not disturbing. The domain is unstated (nothing says the numbers are integers or positive) but the answer is invariant: 42 is the max over the reals and 42 is an integer, so integrality would change nothing. Exclusivity is robust for a second reason worth recording: the implicit constraint L >= s is NOT binding at the optimum (at L = 42, s = 18), so a solver who never imposes it still lands on 42. I looked hard for an option reachable by both a legitimate reading and an error path and did not find one - 'at least 12 more than the larger' admits only 3s >= L + 12 in English; 48 needs the constant moved to the wrong side, 54 needs reporting 3s instead of 60 - s, and both are errors, not readings. Every option is a legal candidate on magnitude: the larger of two numbers summing to 60 must lie in [30, 60), and 30/42/48/54 all do, so nothing is eliminable by kind or size. One small internal tension to flag rather than fix: the explanation treats L = 30 as admissible ('the smallest the larger number can be'), which requires reading 'the larger' non-strictly, while the stem's 'the smaller number / the larger number' phrasing invites a strict reading under which L > 30. This does not touch the key or exclusivity, but under the strict reading the 30 distractor becomes eliminable with no algebra, which is why I graded the set plausible rather than strong. Difficulty: one linear inequality after a substitution, with the real work being the direction flip (maximize L <=> minimize s) - that is the median hard-route item, not the top of it.

ALG-H4-22.new_tell: Two, both mild and both about the option set rather than the stem. (1) The choices are 1, 2, 3, 4 - consecutive integers from 1 - which hands over the scale of the answer before any work: the student learns the crossing must fall within the first handful of months and can stop searching. (2) The crossing value itself (60/15 = 4) sits in the option set. A test-wise student who computes only 60/15 = 4 and applies the convention 'strictly-below-a-clean-crossing means crossing minus one' selects 3 without ever evaluating m = 1, 2, 3. That is still algebra, so it is not a leak, but the key is recoverable from a single division plus a habit.
ALG-H4-22.note: Clean on both defects it was checked for. The count is bounded with no stated ceiling needed: 60 + 45m > 60m fails for all large m because the 60/month model overtakes, so 'm is at least 1' with no upper limit still yields a finite answer - the domain is open above but the solution set is not, which is the right way to leave it. Exclusivity turns entirely on 'greater than' being strict, and the stem says greater than, so m = 4 (where both totals are 300) is excluded on the plain reading; 4 is defensible only by substituting >= for >, which is an error rather than an alternative reading. I checked for the two-route defect specifically: no option is reachable both legitimately and by mistake. 1, 2 and 4 each have exactly one documented error path (wrong divisor, off-by-one start, non-strict comparison) and none of the three has a second, legitimate reading behind it. Every option is a legal candidate - all four are plausible counts of a small integer set, none is the wrong sort of quantity and none is excluded by anything the stem fixes - so nothing falls out by kind or magnitude. The nearest thing to a free elimination is m = 1 (105 vs 60 is one addition), but ruling the ANSWER 1 out still requires testing m = 2, so it costs arithmetic. Difficulty is the one place I would push back on the batch's own label: the modelling is two straight-line costs with friendly numbers, the inequality collapses to 60 > 15m in one step, and the only friction is the strict-inequality count. For the second module a strong student sees, that is an easy item, not a hard one. If this slot needs to carry hard, the fix is in the model (a per-month fee that changes after a threshold, or a fee charged on both sides), not in the options - reshuffling or re-keying cannot raise it.
